evidence_quotes.quote: Esses são alguns aspectos encontrados no arranjo federaƟ vo do setor de saneamento, que implicam a falta de acesso de parte considerável da população do país a esse serviço, notadamente nas menores cidades.

criterion_notes.c1: Examines basic sanitation policy (water supply and sewage collection/treatment networks) and household sanitation access deficits in Brazilian municipalities, particularly small cities.
criterion_notes.c2: Plain wording: YES — examines legal, institutional, and governance arrangements in Brazilian sanitation (Art. 23 of the 1988 Constitution, Law 11.445/2007, Law 11.107/2005 on public consortia, PL 4.162/2019, fiscal rules, and federal agency mandates). Narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading: NO — treats federalism, municipal technical/fiscal capacity asymmetries, and fragmentation of federal ministerial programs and budgets as macro-governance policy background rather than analyzing a rule-type mechanism directly governing household or community service access (references to municipal titularity and concession incentives in PL 4.162/2019 are brief, non-empirical legislative commentary).
criterion_notes.c3: Non-empirical narrative literature review and policy/legislative essay supported only by official documents, statutes, and four descriptive background charts from secondary government databases (SNIS 2017, SIGA Brasil, SIOP 2020); contains no primary data, no qualitative or quantitative empirical methodology, and no systematic synthesis method (exclude as E05).
criterion_notes.c4: Does not analyze a service-access outcome in an empirical design; cites a single descriptive secondary chart of state-level percentages of households with treated sewage (SNIS 2017) as background framing alongside administrative indicators (municipal sanitation plans, number of federal agencies with sanitation programs, and federal budget execution).
criterion_notes.c5: Because the article is a narrative policy essay rather than an empirical study, there is no identifiable empirical study design, analytical sample, or evaluated exposure-outcome relationship.
criterion_notes.c6: Published in Portuguese (with Portuguese, English, and Spanish abstracts), which is directly eligible under Criterion 9.

study_design: Narrative literature review and policy overview (non-empirical essay)
population_and_sample: Brazilian municipalities and federal sanitation sector institutions (narrative macro-policy overview citing aggregate secondary statistics from SNIS 2017, SIGA Brasil, and SIOP; no empirical sample)
exposure: Macro-level Brazilian federalist governance architecture, intergovernmental decentralization asymmetries, federal institutional/budgetary fragmentation, and national sanitation legislation (CF/1988 Art. 23, Law 11.445/2007, Law 11.107/2005, PL 4.162/2019)
outcome: No empirically analyzed service-access outcome (cites secondary descriptive SNIS 2017 state-level household treated-sewage coverage as background context alongside municipal planning-instrument prevalence, federal agency counts, and federal budget trends)
rationale: Excluded under E05 (No empirical evidence). Rocha Neto (2022) is a narrative policy essay and literature/legislative overview examining how asymmetries in Brazilian federalism, municipal technical and fiscal weakness, and institutional fragmentation across federal ministries hinder the implementation of national basic sanitation policy. Although it illustrates the policy context with four descriptive charts drawn from secondary government portals (SNIS 2017 state sewage coverage and municipal plan prevalence, SIGA Brasil federal agency counts, and SIOP 2015-2019 federal budget execution), it conducts no primary quantitative, qualitative, or socio-legal empirical research, applies no empirical research design linking an exposure to an access outcome, and is not a systematic empirical synthesis. Additionally, under the 2026-10-13 Criterion 2 clarification, its focus is macro-governance intergovernmental policy background rather than an empirically analyzed rule-type mechanism directly governing household or community service access.
